# One Line Out. Alaska's One Name on the AI Power Pledge

> Cordova sits on Prince William Sound, off the state highway system, with no transmission line to another community.

Published 2026-07-26 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-26/

## The story

One Alaska utility signed. Its wires reach no one else.

281 names on the pledge. One of them is in Alaska.

Cordova Electric Cooperative is filed under Cooperative on the White House signatory page. No Railbelt utility appears on the list as read.

Five commitments. Nobody has to keep them.

USA TODAY and POWER both call the pledge non binding. Twenty three governors signed an addendum promising to implement its principles to the greatest extent possible.

1,566 customers. 18 megawatts. No line out.

Cordova Electric Cooperative runs one diesel plant and two hydroelectric plants. The town is off the state highway system and the cooperative is not connected by transmission line to any other community.

Every megawatt in this story, on one axis.

It passed the Senate. Then it stopped.

SB 250 would have required commission approved contracts so a data center's infrastructure and service costs are borne by the operator rather than shifted to other customers. It passed the Alaska Senate on May 16, 2026 and died in House Community and Regional Affairs.

A pledge asks. A contract binds.

The other answer is to leave the grid entirely.

Rep. Nick Begich of Alaska introduced the DATA Act on April 21, 2026. He says it lets manufacturers run on fully self contained grid of one power systems.

A promise is not an instrument.

Twenty three governors signed. One Alaska utility signed, as the list read 2026-07-26. Neither signature is a rule.

## What we verified

- Gov. Mike Dunleavy of Alaska is one of 23 Republican governors who signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge addendum announced on July 23, 2026. [Republican Governors Association](https://www.rga.org/republican-governors-sign-president-trumps-ratepayer-protection-pledge/), primary document, 2026-07-23.
- The pledge preamble states that the American people should not be footing the bill for the benefit of private companies. [Republican Governors Association](https://www.rga.org/republican-governors-sign-president-trumps-ratepayer-protection-pledge/), primary document, 2026-07-23.
- The pledge sets five commitments for signing companies, build bring or buy new power supply, pay for new power delivery infrastructure, pay whether they use the power or not, invest in local jobs and workforce development, and contribute to grid and community resilience. [The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/ratepayer-protection-pledge/), primary document, 2026-07-26.
- EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the global race for AI is underway and America must win it, but not by asking working families to pay for it. [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/president-trump-expands-historic-ratepayer-protection-pledge-protect-american), primary document, 2026-07-23.
- The pledge was first signed on March 4, 2026 by seven AI companies and hyperscalers, Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI. [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/president-trump-expands-historic-ratepayer-protection-pledge-protect-american), primary document, 2026-07-23.
- Read live on July 26, 2026 the White House signatory page counters showed All 281, Cooperatives 176, Utilities 69 and Data Center Developers 35. [The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/ratepayer-protection-pledge/), primary document, 2026-07-26.

# On File, Off Record. Alaska's AI Governor Race.

> 24 days.

Published 2026-07-25 by Alaska AI. 10 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-25/

## What we verified

- Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has brought in 1.8 million dollars since entering Alaska's governor race in February 2026. [source](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/07/23/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-18-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians/), report.
- Treg Taylor reported 1 million dollars in fundraising and Adam Crum reported raising nearly 940,000 dollars. [source](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/07/23/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-18-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians/), report.
- Kreiss-Tomkins said Alaska should have a process and a policy on data centers and that until it does, nothing should happen. [source](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/07/23/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-18-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians/), report.
- Kreiss-Tomkins wants Alaska to hold AI companies liable for harms caused by their products, ban deepfakes, require the disclosure of AI in political ads, crack down on AI enabled fraud, implement protections for children against AI content, and require a human behind state decisions. [source](https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-07-24/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-1-8-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians), report.
- Kreiss-Tomkins said he is a huge supporter of campaign finance reform because he does not think fundraising should have the role that it does, but that in the system we have, it is important. [source](https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-07-24/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-1-8-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians), report.
- Kreiss-Tomkins said most of his national donors have only one agenda, which is whether he can win. [source](https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-07-24/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-1-8-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians), report.
- Kreiss-Tomkins said that almost universally, if donors think someone can win, then national interest starts to appear. [source](https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-07-24/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-1-8-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians), report.
- Alaska's statewide primary election is August 18, 2026. [source](https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-07-24/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-1-8-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians), report.
- No other candidate in the race had reported spending over 650,000 dollars at the time of the filings. [source](https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-07-24/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-1-8-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians), report.
- No allegation of unlawful or improper contributions is reported in this coverage. [source](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/07/23/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-18-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians/), report.
- In a June 2026 candidate survey, Kreiss-Tomkins wrote that at the end of the day it has to be people, not algorithms, making the decisions that shape our lives. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is among the 17 candidates in Alaska's governor race. [source](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/07/23/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-18-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians/), report.
- In the same survey Kreiss-Tomkins wrote that Alaskans' personal information belongs to Alaskans alone and should not be fed into third party systems without consent. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- In the same survey Kreiss-Tomkins wrote that Alaska's power and water are not a giveaway and that no Alaskan should watch their electric bill climb to subsidize a server farm. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- In the same survey Kreiss-Tomkins wrote that he worries the AI industry has downplayed the risks posed to the public and that the federal government has been totally flat footed. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- Republican candidate Michael Gilbert answered the survey by saying he will not use any AI in his administration. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- Mat-Su borough mayor Edna DeVries ended her survey answer on AI by disclosing that she used AI to write it. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- Republican candidate Shelley Hughes says she authored the first AI legislation in Alaska a few years ago. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- Republican candidate Lesil McGuire said any algorithmic decision affecting Alaskans must have an explainable, human appealable path, and that every public facing AI output must be reviewed and signed off by a qualified state employee before release. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- Independent candidate Bill Walker said manufactured ideas cannot substitute genuine, dynamic thought or input from Alaskans. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Treg Taylor and Adam Crum and independent Meda DeWitt did not respond to the survey's questions despite multiple requests. [source](https://www.northernjournal.com/alaska-governors-race-survey-ai-policy-and-news-sources/), report.
- The Air Force issued a request for lease proposals making about 4,700 acres at Joint Base Elmendorf Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station available for AI data center development. [source](https://www.airandspaceforces.com/usaf-land-ai-data-centers-three-alaska-bases/), report.
- Kreiss-Tomkins reported the largest haul in the field, ahead of Matt Heilala at nearly 1.6 million dollars and Tom Begich at 1.1 million dollars. [source](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/07/23/democrat-in-alaskas-governor-race-reports-18-million-fundraising-haul-driven-by-californians/), report.

[source](https://www.highergov.com/contract-opportunity/rflp-artificial-intelligence-ai-data-center-deve-afcec-26-r-0006-o-db695/), report.

# The Giveaway, Surveyed. Alaska's Free Land for AI

> Alaska is moving to hand 31 square miles of public land to its own development agency for zero dollars.

Published 2026-07-22 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-22/

## The story

31 SQUARE / MILES OF / PUBLIC LAND. / FREE.

The state moved to give it to its own development agency.

19,950 acres. / No price.

Under a preliminary decision, a state agency would convey about 19,950 acres of public land, roughly 31 square miles, to AIDEA, the state development authority. The site sits two miles north of Houston. Case ADL 234762.

What the land is for

The plan is a multi-use industrial and energy district, and scalable data centers are named among the uses, per the project decision and local coverage. Data centers are the physical plant of modern AI. Free land is meant to pull them in.

Alaska has 8. / Virginia has 639.

Alaska has 8 data centers, among the fewest of any state. Virginia has 639. The state sees a hole to fill, and cheap public land is one lever it can pull.

Not answering demand. / Building it.

This is build it and they will come, aimed at a public asset. Free land is the subsidy, spent before a single data center exists.

The town next door says no

Houston City Council member Lisa Johansen has proposed banning data centers inside city limits. But the state parcel sits about two miles north of Houston, outside the line a town of a few thousand can draw. The town can zone itself, not the land next door.

The choice was never data centers or nothing.

It is the terms. Free or priced. Who zones it, who profits, and who carries the cost if the servers never come. Right now it is only a boundary on a map, which is what a comment period is for.

It is not decided yet

This is a preliminary decision. Public comment on case ADL 234762 runs through 5:00 p.m. on Wednesday, August 19, 2026. If nothing significant changes, the state can then issue it as the final finding and decision.

Comment before Aug 19

Read case ADL 234762 and tell the state what 31 square miles of public land is worth. That is the one price control left before this goes final. Should the state give public land away to attract data centers, or set a price the town next door helps decide?

# A Better Ear Is Not a Recovery

> Cook Inlet has about 331 belugas left, and AI can finally hear them through the ship noise.

Published 2026-07-21 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-21/

## The story

Now a machine can hear them through the ship noise.

Two gates. One white whale.

NOAA Fisheries, Microsoft AI for Good and Alaska Fish and Game built a deep learning listener in two stages. Stage one flags a sound. Stage two names the species behind it.

Down almost 80 percent.

Cook Inlet's belugas are a genetically distinct population, cut off from every other Alaska stock. They fell from about 1,300 whales in 1979 to 279 by 2018, and were listed endangered in 2008.

A whale in a wall of noise.

Ocean noise is one of the biggest threats NOAA lists for these belugas. In a crowded inlet a single call can vanish under a passing ship. Hearing them at all is the first problem.

It learns the calls it used to miss.

The model uses contrastive audio language models and active learning. It sorts a sound into beluga, killer whale or humpback, flags the calls it is unsure of for a person to label, and firms up a daily read of where belugas are.

Ears below. Eyes above.

A separate NOAA led effort, with the U.S. Geological Survey, Microsoft AI for Good and the Naval Research Laboratory, is teaching a cloud model to spot the same whales in satellite images.

331 today. Still far below 1979.

The machine measures the whale. It cannot move it.

A sharper ear tells managers where and when the belugas are. It does not quiet the ships, refill the prey, or clear the inlet. The hunt has been closed since 2007, and the whales still have not recovered.

A better ear is not a recovery.

AI can finally hear Alaska's most endangered whale. What would it take to bring it back?

Slides and the deck PDF are linked from the canonical page.

# Reading the Frozen Ground at the Top of America

> Under one road in Utqiagvik, the northernmost US city, two buried cables now teach the frozen ground to forecast its own thaw.

Published 2026-07-19 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-19/

## The story

The frozen ground now forecasts itself

Two buried cables. Three winters of data. One Alaska road.

Two cables. One road. A kilometer each.

Under one road embankment in Utqiagvik, the northernmost city in the United States, a Penn State team buried a pair of fiber-optic cables, each 1 km (0.6 mi) long, to feel the ground.

Warming ground breaks what we build on it

Permafrost worldwide is warming, by up to almost 2 F per decade. If the thaw holds, Arctic communities could see billions in damaged roads, pipes, and buildings. The old answer is to guess. The new one is to measure.

The wire that listens to frost

For 33 months, the cables read temperature and seismic motion straight from the embankment. Terabytes of ground, recorded in the dark.

A live twin, fed by the buried cables

They fused physics equations with machine learning to build a digital twin, a real-time simulation of that embankment, fed by the cables. This is narrow, physics-informed AI, not a general or generative one.

DIGITAL TWIN / UTQIAGVIK EMBANKMENT

Not a smarter guess. A guess the ground corrects.

Each forecast meets the next real reading, and the gap teaches the model. The value is not certainty. It is a prediction the frozen ground itself keeps grading, season after season.

One kilometer, lit. The rest is dark ground.

This models one embankment, not the North Slope. The team says the method is broadly transferable, which is a claim, not a deployment.

Fund a decade more of ground truth?

The lead researcher wants about 10 more years of data, an aspiration, not a funded plan. So the real question for Alaska, keep the wire in the ground, or harden the roads we already know are failing?

# Alaska's Critical Mineral Engine, and Its Unbuilt AI

> Alaska just won a decade-scale federal bet to find its critical minerals. The AI headlining it is one unbuilt sentence.

Published 2026-07-15 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-15/

## The story

IT ISN'T BUILT YET

THE NSF JUST FUNDED AN AI TO FIND ALASKA'S CRITICAL MINERALS

Alaska just won one of 12 new federal Innovation Engines.

NSF named a University of Alaska Fairbanks coalition its Critical Mineral Accelerator Engine. It opens with 15 million dollars for the first two years. Far more can follow, only if it delivers.

56 of the 60 minerals the U.S. calls essential are in this ground.

That is the U.S. Geological Survey count, essential to the nation's economy and its security. Alaska is not short on critical minerals. It is short on knowing exactly where, in a place this big.

Read the ground. Find the deposits. Pull the minerals out.

The Engine pairs advanced mining, processing and purification with two newer ideas, artificial intelligence to help locate mineral deposits, and new biological methods to extract them. This is what a prospectivity model would draw, if one existed.

It is announced and funded in principle. It is not yet specified. That is not a scandal. It is the stage this is at.

It is a ladder, not a check.

Seven minerals the announcement names.

One site is named so far. The rest is still a search.

The only location named so far is Alaska Silver's exploration site in western Alaska. NANA Regional Corporation is a partner, not an owner. UAF leads it, with geoscientist Lee Ann Munk as chief executive. The goal, cut U.S. dependence on China for mineral processing.

# The Anchorage Address

> An Alaska Native-owned firm just won a $24.96M Navy contract for autonomous stealth boats. They will be built in Oregon.

Published 2026-07-14 by Alaska AI. 8 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-14/

## The story

The boat is Alaskan. The shipyard is not.

An Anchorage, Native-owned firm won a $24.96M Navy contract for autonomous stealth vessels. They will be built in Oregon.

The Navy did not shop around.

AMOUNT $24,960,408 · FOR autonomous low-profile vessels · TO ReconCraft LLC, Anchorage, Alaska · BUILT IN Clackamas, Oregon · DONE BY November 2028 · BOUGHT sole source, no competition · PAID FROM FY2026 innovative technologies (Navy)

Built to show almost nothing.

FREEBOARD under 0.61 m · LENGTH about 19.75 m (65 ft) · PAYLOAD 2,000 to 4,627 kg · RANGE about 2,200 nautical miles. The hull is borrowed from narco-submarines, tuned to beat radar, sonar, sight and heat.

No crew. Not yet a mind.

What the Navy wants next, run itself in crowded ports, with GPS jammed and comms down. What it does today, no one aboard, driven by remote control and pre-set waypoints. Autonomous is the plan, not yet the whole reality.

A set-aside did the winning.

The Navy bought this sole source under the SBA 8(a) program, the federal channel that routes contracts to Native-owned and disadvantaged small firms. Native-owned, tribally owned, 8(a) certified through Dec 2, 2026. The program is doing what it was built to do.

Owned up here. Welded down there.

ANCHORAGE, ALASKA, incorporated here, Native-owned, the address on the contract. CLACKAMAS, OREGON, the shipyard, where the steel is actually cut, hulls up to 120 ft. Two states, one boat, one flag on the contract.

Alaska's seat in the robot-boat boom is an ownership stake, not a shipyard.

That is a real Alaska Native business win. It is also most of what Alaska's slice looks like right now.

An Alaska industry, or just an Alaska address?

If a Native-owned firm wins the contract but the boats are built Outside, does the win count as Alaska's? Tell me where you land. Sources in the comments.

# The Interior's Power Math

> Golden Valley Electric's board weighs $120 million in new gas capacity today, and its members carry the debt.

Published 2026-07-13 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-13/

## The story

$120 million. One vote today. Members own the bill.

a co-op decides behind a closed door

A turbine, and a $120 million question

On July 13, in a closed executive session, Golden Valley Electric Association's board weighs buying a second LM6000 gas turbine for its North Pole plant. The price is about $120 million. In April the board spent $50,000 just to hold a place in the order line.

The News-Miner reports demand for these turbines has surged because large data centers need a guaranteed power supply.

One machine. Steel and megawatts.

An LM6000 makes 45 to 58 megawatts on its own, or 76 to 152 paired with steam or storage. The plant's first LM6000, from 2006, still runs at 47 megawatts. Ordering another can take three to five years.

Members just absorbed the biggest fuel hike on record.

On June 1 the fuel charge jumped 61 percent, the largest increase GVEA has ever posted. The fuel its plants burn more than doubled since February.

The loads are still on paper.

The Air Force is offering about 4,700 acres, 12 parcels across three bases, to companies that would build AI data centers. Two of them, Eielson and Clear, are in the Interior. None is built, no lease is signed. A pending defense bill would require a grid study, if it becomes law.

Firm power, soft load.

The bill is certain. The load is a maybe.

Members are being asked to finance firm, dated capacity now, while the loads that justify it stay on paper. And the vote happens in executive session, a room members reach only through board elections.

Should a co-op spend $120 million on firm power while the loads that need it are still proposals? Or wait until someone signs for the load?

# One River, Two Ways to Count It, AI vs the Tower

> A hand-clicker on a Bristol Bay tower has counted the sockeye since 1955. This year an AI drone wants that job.

Published 2026-07-09 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-09/

## What we verified

- An autonomous drone-in-a-box launches at 8:30 a.m. on an automated flight to an observation position above the right bank of the Wood River. source, report.
- Project lead Norm Van Vactor says he has been engaged in the Bristol Bay commercial fishery for 40 years. source, report.
- Ian Chiu develops the machine-learning components of the project remotely. source, report.
- Van Vactor calls the moment an 'amazing convergence of technology,' citing drone-in-a-box, machine learning and AI, Starlink Mini, lithium batteries and solar panels all maturing in the last year or two. source, report.
- The 2026 Bristol Bay preseason forecast estimates a total run of 44.05 million sockeye. source, report.
- As of July 6, 2026, the total Bristol Bay sockeye run to date was 26,944,183 fish. source, report.
- As of the July 6, 2026 report, Wood River tower escapement to date totaled 2,112,834 fish. source, report.
- Wood River tower crews counted 57,258 sockeye on Sunday. source, report.
- The Wood River escapement goal range is 700,000 to 2.8 million fish, and the 2026 run is within that range. source, report.
- The story was written by Jessie Sheldon and republished statewide via KMXT on July 8, 2026 (originally KDLG, July 3, 2026). source, report.
- The drone imagery is fed into a computer model intended to generate more accurate salmon escapement counts. source, report.
- Machine-learning developer Ian Chiu describes the end product as a computer vision model trained to pick out salmon from video. source, report.
- The team will likely need several thousand drone images to train the model to reliably identify a fish; technicians hand-label the imagery. source, report.
- Alaska Department of Fish and Game has used counting towers for Bristol Bay escapement since 1955 (70+ years). source, report.
- Tower crews rotate through continuous 24-hour shifts, counting each passing salmon with a hand-clicker in 10-minute intervals. source, report.
- Most Bristol Bay escapement counts currently come from nine Fish & Game counting tower sites. source, report.
- Project partners include the University of Washington's Fisheries Research Institute (lab at Lake Aleknagik), the Bristol Bay Regional Seafood Development Association, and the Bristol Bay Economic Development Corporation. source, report.
- At this stage, Alaska Department of Fish and Game is not directly involved in the drone project. source, report.

Slides and the deck PDF are linked from the canonical page.

# Alaska's AI Land Rush, Four Rooms, One Open Door

> Alaska got more than 500 public comments on a $10 billion North Slope AI data center. Fewer than a dozen said yes.

Published 2026-07-08 by Alaska AI. 9 slides.
Canonical: https://alaskaaihq.com/archive/2026-07-08/

## What we verified

- More than 500 public comments were submitted to Alaska DNR on the Stak Energy lease before the preliminary deadline. source, report.
- Fewer than a dozen of the public comments endorsed the Stak project. source, report.
- DNR extended the ADL 422741 public comment deadline to 4:30 p.m. Alaska Daylight Time on July 17, 2026 (extension notice ID 224224). source, report.
- The original comment deadline on the Stak preliminary decision was 4:30 p.m. on June 15, 2026 (original notice ID 223817, published May 12, 2026). source, report.
- DNR said it extended the comment period because of significant public interest, comment volume, and requests for extension. source, report.
- DNR's Division of Oil and Gas issued a preliminary decision to offer STAK Energy Corporation a 50-year lease. source, report.
- The proposed lease covers a 715.4-acre parcel of state land. source, report.
- The parcel sits adjacent to the Dalton Highway approximately 26 miles south of Deadhorse. source, report.
- The docket is ADL 422741 with applicant STAK Energy Corporation; notice 223817 (published May 12, 2026) is the original preliminary decision notice and notice 224224 (published June 17, 2026) is the extension notice. source, report.
- Stak's John Boyle said the full project would cost more than $10 billion. source, report.
- Stak estimated approximately $500 million for initial site evaluation, engineering, gravel road and pad construction, and initial camp and support infrastructure. source, report.
- Stak proposes 1 to 3 gigawatts of on-site natural gas-fired generation. source, report.
- Northern Journal reports that a gigawatt of generation is some 30% more than the peak demand of urban Alaska's entire grid. source, report.
- Lease documents indicate full simple-cycle operation could consume roughly 350 to 500 million standard cubic feet of gas per day. source, report.
- That daily gas burn annualizes to approximately 128 to 183 billion cubic feet per year. source, report.
- The project would require roughly 7.1 million cubic yards of gravel fill. source, report.
- Plans include a roughly 640-acre gravel pad. source, report.
- Plans include a 1.8-mile gravel access road. source, report.
- John Boyle said most comments were form letters lacking substance. source, report.
- John Boyle is Stak's chief strategy officer and previously served as commissioner of Alaska's Department of Natural Resources from 2023 to 2025. source, report.
- Opposition comments carried subject lines including 'HELL NO! To ANY DATA CENTERS' and 'NO AI'. source, report.
- One commenter urged the state to 'incorporate some AI (Alaskan intelligence) into making this decision'. source, report.
- One commenter noted their message was written 'with my own brain and fingers typing'. source, report.
- Comments arrived from Kodiak, Kotzebue, Seward, Valdez, and the North Slope village of Nuiqsut. source, report.
- Formal opposition or concern also came from the Northern Alaska Environmental Center, the Alaska Public Interest Research Group, and the Alaska chapter of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. source, report.
- According to Stak, average annual temperatures at the proposed site are 12 F. source, report.
- Stak expects the development to need 10% or less of the water that typical data centers use for cooling. source, report.
- After the deadline passes, DNR will assess the comments before making a final decision on the lease. source, report.
- Stak said in a statement that it 'is committed to being a responsible steward of the land entrusted to us'. source, report.
- The Department of the Air Force is offering approximately 4,700 acres of underutilized land at JBER, Eielson AFB, and Clear Space Force Station for AI data centers. source, report.
- Twelve parcels have been identified for potential development under the program. source, report.
- The Air Force announced the Alaska AI data center Enhanced Use Lease opportunity on April 10, 2026. source, report.
- The Air Force released its Request for Lease Proposal on June 5, 2026. source, report.
- Developer lease proposals were due June 29, 2026. source, report.
- The RFLP identifies five potential parcels in the Eielson AFB area. source, report.
- Four parcels are under consideration around Clear Space Force Station, including one that would connect to the GVEA grid from the Parks Highway. source, report.
- One Eielson-area parcel is less than a mile from North Pole Middle School. source, report.
- Resident Sarah Hollister said living near data centers is described as like having a vacuum cleaner running around the clock. source, report.
- Sarah Hollister raised concern about data center heat discharge affecting permafrost. source, report.
- Hollister pointed out that three of the proposed sites would be expected to use the GVEA grid and asked whether that would affect members' bills. source, report.
- JBER commander Col. Lisa Mabbutt said Alaska is expected to receive up to $8 billion in Air Force investments over the next five years. source, report.
- Under Secretary of the Air Force Matthew Lohmeier toured JBER and Eielson AFB June 22 through 24, 2026. source, report.
- GVEA recommended that any major loads be connected to its 138-kilovolt line. source, report.
- The Air Force plans to choose proposals that minimize and mitigate impact and risk to the surrounding community, with utilities remaining accessible and affordable. source, report.
- GVEA's board will weigh whether to invest in a fuel-based generator during an executive session on July 13, 2026. source, report.
- A new LM6000 unit would cost GVEA about $120 million. source, report.
- An LM6000 can generate between 45 and 58 megawatts depending on the model. source, report.
- Costs to construct a new gas turbine power plant jumped 195% from 2019 to 2026, per a Bloomberg News report cited by the News-Miner. source, report.
- Turbine order waitlists have pushed into the early 2030s, per a Bloomberg News report cited by the News-Miner. source, report.
- Demand for the turbine units has increased due to a surge in large data centers that require a guaranteed power supply, per a Bloomberg News report. source, report.
- At its April 2026 board meeting, GVEA approved $50,000 to reserve an order spot for an LM6000 combined-cycle turbine. source, report.
- GVEA's fuel and purchased power charge rose by about 61 percent effective June 1, 2026. source, report.
- The increase costs the average residential member nearly $46 more per month. source, report.
- GVEA's power plant fuel prices roughly doubled from about $2.50 to $5.10 per gallon. source, report.
- House-Senate conference committee members unveiled a draft compromise AKLNG tax bill on Thursday, July 2, 2026. source, report.
- The draft compromise would replace the state's property tax with a volumetric tax on gas after five years of operation or once flow reaches 500 million cubic feet per day, whichever comes first. source, report.
- The draft extends the construction completion deadline for the gas line and phase one from 2032 to December 31, 2034. source, report.
- Phase one of the project is an 807-mile gas line from the North Slope to Cook Inlet. source, report.
- Glenfarne owns 75% of the Alaska LNG project. source, report.
- Lawmakers are tentatively planning House and Senate floor votes on the compromise bill for Thursday, July 16, 2026. source, report.
- Lawmakers are in a second special session called by Gov. Mike Dunleavy, scheduled to end July 19, 2026. source, report.
- Dunleavy has called the corporate income tax provision a 'poison pill' and pledged to veto any bill that includes it. source, report.
- The governor and the developer have said the S corp tax in the draft will hurt the project's ability to secure financing. source, report.
- On the Wood River, an automated drone emerges from its box at exactly 8:30 a.m. and takes off on an automated flight path. source, report.
- The team expects to need several thousand drone images for the computer-vision model to learn to reliably identify a fish. source, report.
- Alaska Fish and Game has been tracking salmon escapement since 1955. source, report.
- Tower technicians count each passing salmon with a hand-clicker in 10-minute intervals. source, report.
- Tower crews rotate through continuous shifts over 24 hours. source, report.
- Most escapement counts across Bristol Bay currently come from nine Fish and Game counting tower sites. source, report.
- The pilot is run with the University of Washington's Fisheries Research Institute, the Bristol Bay Regional Seafood Development Association, and the Bristol Bay Economic Development Corporation. source, report.
- Norm Van Vactor is a project lead on the drone counting pilot. source, report.
- In the project's next phase, the crew will test their models against Fish and Game tower counting data. source, report.
- BBRSDA's drone salmon-monitoring project received a $70,000 Seafood Industry Climate Award grant from the Acme Smoked Fish Foundation. source, report.
- According to the funder, the drone project enables managers to detect salmon run timing up to 24 hours earlier. source, report.
- The 2026 preseason forecast expects a Bristol Bay total run of 44.05 million sockeye. source, report.
- The Bristol Bay run had reached 17,011,218 sockeye through July 1, 2026, as reported July 2. source, report.
- Wood River tower crews counted 123,489 sockeye on Wednesday, July 1, bringing their cumulative count to 1,884,747 fish. source, report.
- Alaska's 2026 primary election is August 18, 2026. source, report.
- Incumbent Gov. Mike Dunleavy is term-limited and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. source, report.
- Alaska saw over 9,000 lightning strikes in a single day in late June 2026, amid a week of prolific lightning. source, report.
- A U.S. Forest Service Uncrewed Aircraft System module from Boise, Idaho was assigned to fly reconnaissance, mapping, and infrared missions on the Polly Fire. source, report.
- The Cecil Fire is approximately 724 acres and 100% contained, with 18 personnel assigned, as of July 6, 2026. source, report.
- A UAS drone flight on July 6, 2026 detected no remaining heat on the Cecil Fire. source, report.
- A permafrost digital twin under a Utqiagvik road embankment was built from a pair of one-kilometer fiber-optic cables that collected temperature and seismic data from September 2021 to June 2024. source, report.
- The digital twin approach more accurately predicted the embankment permafrost's unfrozen water content, ground temperature changes, and heat movement. source, report.
